doc_summary: Greenblatt proposes IDSS, an iterative strategy of building and studying weak, easy-to-catch schemers as testbeds, then scaling detection and mitigation techniques up capability rungs. He stresses analogousness to dangerous schemers, cheap iteration, and failure modes of the inductive scheme.

items.claim: Prefers testing on weak, cheap-to-experiment-on schemers that are iteratively scaled up over studying only natural powerful schemers because natural examples are hard to catch, re-catch and obtain in diversity.
items.quote: Two key difficulties with using natural examples of scheming are that it is hard to catch (and re-catch) schemers and that it’s hard to (cheaply) get a large number of diverse examples of scheming to experiment on.

items.claim: Prefers testbeds that are analogous to the dangerous target over testbeds that merely elicit the behavior, because rigging training to induce scheming can make the examples less representative.
items.quote: We can potentially try to rig the training of these weak AIs we’re using for our experiments to make scheming more likely, but this might make these schemers even less analogous.

items.claim: Relaxes artificial easy-to-catch constraints as detection improves, trading off catchability against analogousness to improve how realistic the testbed is.
items.quote: We can also relax the extent to which we need to train the schemers to be easy to catch (improving analogousness) as we develop better detection techniques.

items.claim: Starts evidence collection with basic behavioral testing and chain-of-thought inspection for weak schemers, while worrying these may not scale to powerful schemers.
items.quote: it might be hard to mostly-continuously scale from detection techniques that work on weak schemers (basic behavioral testing, look at the chain-of-thought) up to techniques that will suffice for powerful models.

items.claim: Distrusts transfer of findings from weak to strong models when analogousness is insufficient, expecting results to generalize only to slightly more capable models by continuity.
items.quote: By continuity, we hope that all of these approaches generalize to slightly more capable AIs (even if they wouldn’t generalize much to the AIs we actually care about just yet due to insufficient analogousness).

items.claim: Doubts that one can get high confidence the method works, and emphasizes open questions about how analogous the constructed schemers actually were.
items.quote: Exactly how analogous were those scheming AIs we made? How exactly did we ultimately end up with detection techniques which worked well enough for our most powerful AIs?

items.claim: Frames the strategy as an inductive argument and diagnoses failures by base case, inductive step and discontinuities, judging the inductive step as the likely hardest.
items.quote: My current sense is that the difficulty is probably mostly in the inductive step, because scheming will just get harder to experiment on as AIs get more capable.

items.claim: Treats misalignment involving deliberate faking of alignment as qualitatively harder to study than other failure modes like reward hacking, which can be studied more straightforwardly.
items.quote: other misalignment failure modes can probably be studied more straightforwardly with other mechanisms as these other failure modes don’t involve the AI carefully trying to fake alignment.

items.claim: Plans follow-up work on concrete, principled removal and prevention techniques to study with improved testbeds.
items.quote: I’m planning to write something about concrete and principled ideas for removal and prevention techniques that we could study.
